passages.happening:
‘A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth’ (verse 1). ‘It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart’ (verse 2). ‘The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure’ (verse 4). The laughter of fools is like thorns crackling under a pot (verse 6).

‘The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one’ (verse 8). ‘Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool’ (verse 9). Do not ask why the old days were better than these (verse 10). Wisdom is a shelter, like money, and it preserves the life of its owner (verse 12).

‘Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?’ (verse 13). ‘In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 ended by asking who knows what is good for a person. Chapter 7 answers in part with a string of ‘better’ sayings, like those in Proverbs. The word good, tov, appears eleven times in this chapter. But the Teacher tests this traditional wisdom against what he has seen, and he finds that it does not explain everything. The second half of the book has begun, and the question has shifted from what people gain to what people can know.

When someone died, relatives and neighbors gathered for days of lament, often joined by professional mourners. The Teacher says it is better to go there than to a feast, because there a person has to face the truth that death comes to everyone. These sayings ask for a sober, clear-eyed life. They are not a wish to die.

Verse 1 is a play on sounds: name, shem, is better than perfume, shemen. Perfume was a luxury, and its scent faded. A good name outlasted it. Verse 6 is another: thorns, sirim, crackle under a pot, sir. Dry thornbushes burned fast and loud and gave little lasting heat.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Job's friend asks the question of verse 13 in his own way: ‘Can you fathom the deep things of God’ (Job 11:7), he says. And Job accepted the two kinds of days of verse 14: “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” (Job 2:10).
passages.asks: The Teacher says the house of mourning teaches more than the house of feasting. Ask what you have learned at a funeral that you would not have learned at a party. And ask how you might receive both the good days and the hard days as from God's hand.

passages.happening:
‘In my futile life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness’ (verse 15).

‘Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?’ (verse 16). ‘Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?’ (verse 17). Hold on to both warnings, ‘For he who fears God will follow both warnings’ (verse 18).

‘Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city’ (verse 19). And then: “Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (verse 20). So do not listen to every word people say about you. You may hear a servant cursing you, ‘For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 15 is the Teacher's honest report of what Proverbs' patterns cannot explain.

Verses 16 and 17 have puzzled readers. They are not a call to sin a little, since verse 17 warns just as plainly against wickedness. Set beside verse 20, the warning against being overly righteous can be heard as a warning against trusting one's own righteousness, since no one on earth is without sin. The one who fears God avoids both errors.

Verses 21 and 22 are gentle and searching. Do not take every insult to heart, because you have said such things yourself.
passages.later: Paul says the same as verse 20: ‘for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God’ (Romans 3:23). And Solomon prayed it at the temple's dedication: ‘for there is no one who does not sin’ (1 Kings 8:46).
passages.asks: No one is righteous without sin. Ask where you have been counting on your own goodness. And ask whose careless words about you you could let go, remembering your own.

passages.t: Searching, and the little that was found
passages.happening:
The Teacher tested everything by wisdom and resolved to be wise, ‘But it was beyond me’ (verse 23). ‘What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?’ (verse 24). He set his mind to search out wisdom and explanations, and to understand the folly of wickedness (verse 25).

He found something more bitter than death: ‘the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared’ (verse 26).

Then the narrator breaks in briefly, “says the Teacher” (verse 27). Searching and not finding, he found one upright man among a thousand, but not one woman among all those (verse 28). And the one thing he did find is this: ‘God made men upright, but they have sought out many schemes’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The verb to find, matsa, runs all through these verses. The Teacher sought and did not find. A search for complete wisdom ends in an honest admission of failure, and that is the lesson.

Verse 26 echoes Proverbs 5 to 7, where the adulteress leads young men to death, and Proverbs 9, where Folly calls to the simple as a woman.

Verse 27 is one of the few places where the book's second voice, the narrator, steps into the middle of the Teacher's words.
passages.later: Job's poem on wisdom asks the same as verse 24: ‘But where can wisdom be found, and where does understanding dwell?’ (Job 28:12). And the Bible's first word on humanity, behind verse 29, honors man and woman alike: ‘male and female He created them’ (Genesis 1:27).
passages.hard:
What does the Teacher mean by the bitter woman in verse 26, and by not finding one upright woman in a thousand (verse 28)?

These verses are among the most troubling in the book, and interpreters read them in several ways.

Some take them as the Teacher's honest but limited observation, the words of a man in an ancient world where men held power, which Scripture records without endorsing, as it records other conclusions of his that the book later qualifies. Others argue that the woman who is a snare is not women in general but the seductive woman, or Folly, of Proverbs 5 to 9, so that verse 26 warns against folly, not against women. Some note that ‘a thousand’ recalls Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines (1 Kings 11:3), and read the verse as a comment on what that king found in his own household, not a judgment on women. Still others point to verse 29, which uses the general word for humanity, adam, and concludes that God made human beings upright and all have gone astray, so that the search found both men and women wanting. Many readers combine these observations.

What is clear is that the passage's last word indicts humanity as a whole. The rest of Scripture honors women as fully bearing God's image (Genesis 1:27), and Proverbs ends by praising a woman of strength (Proverbs 31). These verses give no one a license for contempt toward women.
passages.asks: The Teacher's search for complete wisdom failed. Ask where you have been trying to understand everything before you will trust God. And ask whether any of your own judgments about whole groups of people need the humility of verse 29.
